claim: Cortical gamma oscillations have been implicated in a variety of cognitive, behavioral, and circuit-level phenomena.
source: Cortical gamma oscillations have been implicated in a variety of cognitive, behavioral, and circuit-level phenomena.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific literature in the field.

claim: The circuit mechanisms of gamma-band generation and synchronization across cortical space remain uncertain.
source: However, the circuit mechanisms of gamma-band generation and synchronization across cortical space remain uncertain.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field prior to the study.

claim: A circuit composed of layer 2/3 (L2/3) pyramidal cells and somatostatin (SOM) interneurons phase-locks ensembles across the retinotopic map.
source: Using optogenetic patterned illumination in acute brain slices of mouse visual cortex, we define a circuit composed of layer 2/3 (L2/3) pyramidal cells and somatostatin (SOM) interneurons that phase-locks ensembles across the retinotopic map.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data using optogenetic manipulation and electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Photo-induced gamma oscillations emerge from non-periodic stimuli.
source: The network oscillations generated here emerge from non-periodic stimuli, and are stimulus size-dependent, coherent across cortical space, narrow band (30 Hz), and depend on SOM neuron but not parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity; similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
evidence: This is directly stated as a characteristic of the photo-induced gamma oscillations observed in the experiments.

claim: Photo-induced gamma oscillations are stimulus size-dependent.
source: The network oscillations generated here emerge from non-periodic stimuli, and are stimulus size-dependent, coherent across cortical space, narrow band (30 Hz), and depend on SOM neuron but not parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity; similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Photo-induced gamma oscillations are coherent across cortical space.
source: The network oscillations generated here emerge from non-periodic stimuli, and are stimulus size-dependent, coherent across cortical space, narrow band (30 Hz), and depend on SOM neuron but not parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity; similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figures 1D-J.

claim: Photo-induced gamma oscillations are narrow band at approximately 30 Hz.
source: The network oscillations generated here emerge from non-periodic stimuli, and are stimulus size-dependent, coherent across cortical space, narrow band (30 Hz), and depend on SOM neuron but not parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity; similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by spectral analysis shown in Figure 1C inset.

claim: Photo-induced gamma oscillations depend on SOM neuron activity.
source: The network oscillations generated here emerge from non-periodic stimuli, and are stimulus size-dependent, coherent across cortical space, narrow band (30 Hz), and depend on SOM neuron but not parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity; similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Photo-induced gamma oscillations do not depend on parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity.
source: The network oscillations generated here emerge from non-periodic stimuli, and are stimulus size-dependent, coherent across cortical space, narrow band (30 Hz), and depend on SOM neuron but not parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity; similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Photo-induced gamma oscillations are similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
source: The network oscillations generated here emerge from non-periodic stimuli, and are stimulus size-dependent, coherent across cortical space, narrow band (30 Hz), and depend on SOM neuron but not parvalbumin (PV) neuron activity; similar to visually induced gamma oscillations observed in vivo.
evidence: This is a comparative statement drawing on similarities between the in vitro findings and previously reported in vivo observations.

claim: Gamma oscillations generated in separate cortical locations exhibited high coherence as far apart as 850 μm.
source: Gamma oscillations generated in separate cortical locations exhibited high coherence as far apart as 850 μm, and lateral gamma entrainment depended on SOM neuron activity.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by dual recording experiments shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Lateral gamma entrainment depends on SOM neuron activity.
source: Gamma oscillations generated in separate cortical locations exhibited high coherence as far apart as 850 μm, and lateral gamma entrainment depended on SOM neuron activity.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: The identified circuit is sufficient to mediate long-range gamma-band coherence in the primary visual cortex.
source: These data identify a circuit that is sufficient to mediate long-range gamma-band coherence in the primary visual cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented throughout the study.

claim: Gamma oscillations (20–80 Hz) within the primary visual cortex (V1) synchronize the activity of functionally related neural ensembles, resulting in their selective amplification in downstream visual areas.
source: It has been proposed that gamma oscillations (20–80 Hz) within the primary visual cortex (V1) synchronize the activity of functionally related neural ensembles, resulting in their selective amplification in downstream visual areas (Fries, 2009; Fries et al., 2007; Singer and Gray, 1995).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: In cats, gamma oscillations recorded in two spatially separated regions in V1 become phase-locked when a continuous visual object occupies their corresponding receptive fields.
source: In cats, gamma oscillations recorded in two spatially separated regions in V1 become phase-locked when a continuous visual object occupies their corresponding receptive fields (Gray et al., 1989; Gray and Singer, 1989).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: In primates, studies have observed strong correlations between gamma power and visual attention.
source: In primates, studies have observed strong correlations between gamma power and visual attention (Fries et al., 2001), as well as increased gamma-band synchrony among visual cortical areas during visual tasks, suggesting a role for gamma oscillations in visual perception and selective attention (Siegel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Increased gamma-band synchrony among visual cortical areas occurs during visual tasks, suggesting a role for gamma oscillations in visual perception and selective attention.
source: In primates, studies have observed strong correlations between gamma power and visual attention (Fries et al., 2001), as well as increased gamma-band synchrony among visual cortical areas during visual tasks, suggesting a role for gamma oscillations in visual perception and selective attention (Siegel et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a finding and interpretation from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: The precise function of gamma rhythms in visual processing remains controversial.
source: However, the precise function of gamma rhythms in visual processing remains controversial, with some studies providing evidence for a role in perceptual coding (Fries, 2009; Pritchett et al., 2015; Salinas and Sejnowski, 2001; Singer and Gray, 1995; Varela et al., 2001; Womelsdorf et al., 2007) and others arguing that neural codes based on the synchrony or phase of spike times during gamma oscillations are unlikely to contribute to visual processing (Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Shadlen and Movshon, 1999; Thiele and Stoner, 2003).
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of debate in the field, supported by citations to conflicting studies.

claim: The cellular and circuit mechanisms underlying long-distance gamma-band coherence are unknown.
source: Since the cellular and circuit mechanisms underlying long-distance gamma-band coherence are unknown, the causal manipulations that could assess whether gamma rhythms are required for key aspects of perception and cognition have yet to be defined.
evidence: This statement reflects the knowledge gap that the study aims to address.

claim: Gamma oscillation generation in the mammalian forebrain typically depends on the reciprocal interaction between nearby recurrently connected excitatory and inhibitory neurons.
source: In the mammalian forebrain, gamma oscillation generation is typically thought to depend on the reciprocal interaction between nearby recurrently connected excitatory and inhibitory neurons, with the precise timing of oscillations depending on the rapid recruitment of inhibitory neurons to transiently and periodically suppress local network activity (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin, 2016; Jefferys et al., 1996; Mann et al., 2005; Tiesinga and Sejnowski, 2009).
evidence: This is a widely accepted model in the field supported by citations.

claim: Fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive (PV) basket cells phase-lock particularly strongly to gamma-band activity in the local field potential.
source: Several studies have correlated the activity of individual subtypes of inhibitory cortical neurons with gamma-paced firing, finding, for instance, that fast-spiking parvalbumin-positive (PV) basket cells phase-lock particularly strongly to gamma-band activity in the local field potential (Bartos et al., 2007; Buzsáki, 2004; Csicsvari et al., 2003; Gulyás et al., 2010; Hasenstaub et al., 2005; Salkoff et al., 2015; Siegle et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from multiple previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Different or multiple inhibitory subtypes are involved in gamma generation and coherence.
source: Other studies have demonstrated that different or multiple inhibitory subtypes are involved in gamma generation and coherence (Craig and McBain, 2015; Kipiani, 2009; Takada et al., 2014; Vierling-Claassen et al., 2010; Whittington et al., 2011), and that gap junctions might also contribute (Ainsworth et al., 2011; Long et al., 2005; Szabadics et al., 2001; Traub et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Gap junctions might contribute to gamma generation and coherence.
source: Other studies have demonstrated that different or multiple inhibitory subtypes are involved in gamma generation and coherence (Craig and McBain, 2015; Kipiani, 2009; Takada et al., 2014; Vierling-Claassen et al., 2010; Whittington et al., 2011), and that gap junctions might also contribute (Ainsworth et al., 2011; Long et al., 2005; Szabadics et al., 2001; Traub et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: In mouse primary visual cortex, somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons contribute to stimulus-size dependent, visually induced oscillations and coherence.
source: Recently, it was also demonstrated that, in mouse primary visual cortex, somatostatin-positive (SOM) interneurons contribute to stimulus-size dependent, visually induced oscillations and coherence (Chen et al., 2017; Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a recent finding from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Dendrite-targeting interneurons might contribute to gamma-band coherence in the hippocampus.
source: Moreover, theoretical work has also suggested that dendrite-targeting interneurons might contribute to gamma-band coherence in the hippocampus (Tort et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a theoretical prediction from previous work supported by a citation.

claim: The cellular and synaptic basis for gamma coherence across the retinotopic map in the visual cortex is poorly understood.
source: Despite this work, the cellular and synaptic basis for gamma coherence across the retinotopic map in the visual cortex is poorly understood.
evidence: This statement reflects the knowledge gap in the field that motivates the study.

claim: Optogenetic stimulation of L2/3 pyramidal cells induces powerful gamma-band oscillations in cortical slices and in vivo.
source: Previously, we and others have shown that optogenetic stimulation of L2/3 pyramidal cells (PCs) induces powerful gamma-band oscillations in cortical slices and in vivo (Adesnik and Scanziani, 2010; Shao et al., 2013; Takada et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies by the authors and others, supported by citations.

claim: ChR2 expression via in utero electroporation is restricted to excitatory neurons.
source: Under these conditions, ChR2 expression is restricted to excitatory neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Adesnik and Scanziani, 2010), and therefore all optogenetically evoked inhibition is driven polysynaptically through the network, rather than being of monosynaptic origin.
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 and a previous citation.

claim: All optogenetically evoked inhibition is driven polysynaptically through the network, rather than being of monosynaptic origin.
source: Under these conditions, ChR2 expression is restricted to excitatory neurons (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Adesnik and Scanziani, 2010), and therefore all optogenetically evoked inhibition is driven polysynaptically through the network, rather than being of monosynaptic origin.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the selective expression of ChR2 in excitatory neurons.

claim: Wide-field illumination of L2/3 generates strong gamma rhythms in excitatory and inhibitory currents measured in L2/3 cortical neurons.
source: Consistent with prior work in both S1 and V1, wide-field illumination of L2/3 generates strong gamma rhythms in excitatory and inhibitory currents measured in L2/3 cortical neurons (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1A,B.

claim: The power of gamma oscillations depends on the area of illumination.
source: Using this system, we found that the power of the gamma oscillations depended on the area of illumination, reminiscent of the dependence of gamma oscillations on visual stimulus size in vivo (Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Jia et al., 2013; Ray et al., 2013; Veit et al., 2017) (Figure 1C. Analyzed from 0 to 1000 ms post-stimulus onset.).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1C, with comparison to in vivo studies.

claim: Photo-stimulation generates gamma oscillations in each illuminated region.
source: Photo-stimulation generated gamma oscillations in each illuminated region, as measured by large oscillatory currents recorded in each cell, and when both sites were co-stimulated, the two oscillations strongly phase-locked (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: When both sites are co-stimulated, the two oscillations strongly phase-lock.
source: Photo-stimulation generated gamma oscillations in each illuminated region, as measured by large oscillatory currents recorded in each cell, and when both sites were co-stimulated, the two oscillations strongly phase-locked (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: Coherence persists even when the recorded cells are separated by up to 850 μm.
source: Coherence persisted even when the recorded cells were separated by up to 850 μm (Figure 1J), demonstrating that photo-induced gamma rhythms can synchronize over long distances.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Photo-induced gamma rhythms can synchronize over long distances.
source: Coherence persisted even when the recorded cells were separated by up to 850 μm (Figure 1J), demonstrating that photo-induced gamma rhythms can synchronize over long distances.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data on long-range coherence.

claim: L2/3 PCs project long-range horizontal axons that traverse the retinotopic map in V1.
source: L2/3 PCs project long-range horizontal axons that traverse the retinotopic map in V1 (Gilbert and Wiesel, 1989) and represent a plausible substrate for synchronizing gamma activity across spatially distant neural ensembles (Gray et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a known anatomical fact supported by a citation.

claim: L2/3 horizontal axons represent a plausible substrate for synchronizing gamma activity across spatially distant neural ensembles.
source: L2/3 PCs project long-range horizontal axons that traverse the retinotopic map in V1 (Gilbert and Wiesel, 1989) and represent a plausible substrate for synchronizing gamma activity across spatially distant neural ensembles (Gray et al., 1989).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on anatomical knowledge and previous observations, supported by citations.

claim: Vertical transection between two recorded cells spares gamma rhythm generation on either side of the cut.
source: This transection spared gamma rhythm generation on either side of the cut, but abolished phase-locking between the two areas (Figure 1G–J; n = 11 pairs, p<10−3, Wilcoxon rank sum test, see figure legend for statistics).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1G-J.

claim: Vertical transection between two recorded cells abolishes phase-locking between the two areas.
source: This transection spared gamma rhythm generation on either side of the cut, but abolished phase-locking between the two areas (Figure 1G–J; n = 11 pairs, p<10−3, Wilcoxon rank sum test, see figure legend for statistics).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by data shown in Figure 1G-J with statistical analysis.

claim: Lateral connections across L2/3 in V1 are necessary for long-range intralaminar gamma coherence.
source: These data demonstrate that lateral connections across L2/3 in V1 are necessary for long-range intralaminar gamma coherence.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the transection experiments showing loss of coherence after cutting L2/3.

claim: Horizontal axons in L2/3 preferentially recruit SOM neurons in vitro.
source: Although substantial evidence implicates PV neurons in gamma entrainment (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009), we previously demonstrated that horizontal axons in L2/3 preferentially recruit SOM neurons in vitro (Adesnik et al., 2012), and that SOM neurons in vivo are also involved in visually induced gamma rhythms (Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: SOM neurons in vivo are involved in visually induced gamma rhythms.
source: Although substantial evidence implicates PV neurons in gamma entrainment (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Cardin et al., 2009; Sohal et al., 2009), we previously demonstrated that horizontal axons in L2/3 preferentially recruit SOM neurons in vitro (Adesnik et al., 2012), and that SOM neurons in vivo are also involved in visually induced gamma rhythms (Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a recent study, supported by a citation.

claim: SOM neurons are reliably driven and tightly correlated with the photo-induced gamma rhythm in L2/3.
source: Strikingly, targeted loose-patch recordings from SOM and PV neurons in brain slices demonstrated that SOM neurons were reliably driven and tightly correlated with the photo-induced gamma rhythm in L2/3 (Figure 2A–C, n = 10 cells, mean induced rate: 25 ± 5 Hz. Data analyzed from 0 to 1000 ms post-stimulation onset.).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The majority of L2/3 PV neurons fire at comparatively low rates or do not fire at all during photo-induced gamma.
source: Under the same conditions, the majority of L2/3 PV neurons fired at comparatively low rates or did not fire at all (4 ± 2 Hz, p=0.003, Wilicoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by electrophysiological data with statistical analysis.

claim: SOM neurons receive powerful, rhythmic excitation but very little inhibition during photo-induced gamma.
source: To probe the basis for this unexpected result, whole-cell recordings from SOM neurons were made and demonstrated that they receive powerful, rhythmic excitation but very little inhibition (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 2D,E.

claim: PV neurons and PCs receive much more synaptic inhibition than SOM neurons during photo-induced gamma.
source: In contrast, PV neurons and PCs received much more synaptic inhibition, consistent with their known inputs from SOM cells (Figure 2D,E; see figure legend for statistics) (Hioki et al., 2013; Pfeffer et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by voltage clamp recordings shown in Figure 2D,E, with comparison to known connectivity patterns.

claim: The large difference in excitation/inhibition ratio provides a synaptic basis for the differential recruitment of SOM and PV neurons during photo-induced gamma.
source: The large difference in their excitation/inhibition ratio provides a synaptic basis for the differential recruitment of SOM and PV neurons during photo-induced gamma.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the E/I ratio data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Local suppression of SOM neurons strongly reduces the inhibitory gamma power observed in PCs during photo-induced gamma activity.
source: Local suppression of SOM neurons strongly reduced the inhibitory gamma power observed in PCs during photo-induced gamma activity (Figure 3A,B mean power reduction: 74 ± 3.5%, p<10−5, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3A,B with statistical analysis.

claim: Suppressing SOM cells desynchronizes excitatory synaptic input during photo-induced gamma.
source: Suppressing SOM cells also desynchronized excitatory synaptic input, demonstrating that their output is critical for pacing the activity of the excitatory network in the gamma band (Figure 3B,C; n = 8 cells, mean power reduction: 63 ± 7%, p=0.004, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3B,C with statistical analysis.

claim: SOM neuron output is critical for pacing the activity of the excitatory network in the gamma band.
source: Suppressing SOM cells also desynchronized excitatory synaptic input, demonstrating that their output is critical for pacing the activity of the excitatory network in the gamma band (Figure 3B,C; n = 8 cells, mean power reduction: 63 ± 7%, p=0.004, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic suppression experiments.

claim: Suppressing PV neurons has no significant effect on gamma power.
source: In contrast, suppressing PV neurons had no significant effect on gamma power (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E, n = 9 cells, mean power reduction: 2.5 ± 6%, p=0.25, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), while it did significantly reduce the disynaptic IPSC to a brief pulse of blue light (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, p=0.016, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 with statistical analysis.

claim: Suppressing PV neurons significantly reduces the disynaptic IPSC to a brief pulse of blue light.
source: In contrast, suppressing PV neurons had no significant effect on gamma power (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E, n = 9 cells, mean power reduction: 2.5 ± 6%, p=0.25, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), while it did significantly reduce the disynaptic IPSC to a brief pulse of blue light (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, p=0.016, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1F with statistical analysis.

claim: Gamma generation within L2/3 critically depends on the activity of SOM neurons.
source: This demonstrates that gamma generation within L2/3 critically depends on the activity of SOM neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the optogenetic suppression experiments showing loss of gamma when SOM neurons are suppressed.

claim: Suppressing SOM cells from before gamma induction abolishes gamma rhythms.
source: We found that suppressing SOM cells from before gamma induction also nearly completely abolished gamma rhythms, indicating that they are required even at the very earliest stages of gamma induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2F-H.

claim: SOM neurons are required even at the very earliest stages of gamma induction.
source: We found that suppressing SOM cells from before gamma induction also nearly completely abolished gamma rhythms, indicating that they are required even at the very earliest stages of gamma induction (Figure 3—figure supplement 2F–H).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the early suppression experiments.

claim: Even at the early stages of gamma, SOM neuron activity far exceeds that of PV neurons.
source: We found that even at the early stages of gamma, SOM neuron activity still far exceeded that of PV neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by spike timing analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-E.

claim: SOM neurons are necessary for both the initiation and maintenance of L2/3-induced gamma oscillations.
source: Although these data do not exclude the possibility that PV neurons could be necessary for oscillatory activity in response to other photo-stimulation protocols, they demonstrate that SOM neurons are necessary for both the initiation and maintenance of L2/3-induced gamma oscillations studied here.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined suppression experiments at different time points.

claim: Horizontally projecting axons of L2/3 PCs might synchronize gamma rhythms across the retinotopic axis of the cortex by synapsing onto laterally located SOM cells.
source: We hypothesized that the horizontally projecting axons of L2/3 PCs might synchronize gamma rhythms across the retinotopic axis of the cortex by synapsing onto laterally located SOM cells, which then enforce phase-locking through their inhibitory output.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on known anatomy and their findings.

claim: Optogenetically suppressing SOM cells local to a phase-locked PC abolishes gamma entrainment.
source: Optogenetic suppression of local SOM neurons with red light abolished phase-locking between PC-spikes and the distally generated gamma oscillation (Figure 4C,D, n = 8 pairs, PPC control: 0.120 ± 0.008; PPC red light: 0.004 ± 0.007, p=0.008, Wilcoxon signed-rank test. Data analyzed from 200 to 1000 ms post-stimulation onset.).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4C,D with statistical analysis.

claim: The activity of SOM neurons outside of the gamma initiation zone is critical for phase-locking spatially separate oscillating ensembles across L2/3 of V1 at least 325 μm apart.
source: Together, these data support the notion that the activity of SOM neurons outside of the gamma initiation zone is critical for phase-locking spatially separate oscillating ensembles across L2/3 of V1 in brain slices at least 325 μm apart.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the lateral suppression experiments in Figure 4.

claim: SOM neurons receive significant, albeit attenuated excitatory input from L2/3 PCs as far away as 450 μm.
source: We found that SOM neurons received significant, albeit attenuated excitatory input from L2/3 PCs as far away as 450 μm (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C, average maximum excitatory current: 120 ± 90 pA, 6 ± 2% of the maximum, n = 9).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by circuit mapping experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: At 450 μm distance, excitatory input to SOM neurons rarely drives spiking on its own.
source: In current clamp, the same neurons reached an average maximal depolarization at 450 μm (calculated in in the final 100 ms of the photo-stimulus) of 7 ± 5 mV (n = 7), which was rarely enough to drive spiking on its own.
evidence: This is directly stated based on current clamp recordings.

claim: Inhibitory currents in L2/3 PCs decay to 4 ± 1% of their maximum at 450 μm distance.
source: At the same time, inhibitory currents in L2/3 PCs decayed to 4 ± 1% of their maximum at the same 450 μm distance (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C, maximum inhibitory current 20 ± 10 pA, n = 8).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by circuit mapping experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: There is no clear evidence of spikelets or subthreshold electrical coupling in SOM neurons that might mediate signal propagation across the retinotopic axis of the cortex.
source: When recording SOM neurons, we did not observe any clear spikelets or evidence of subthreshold electrical coupling that might mediate signal propagation between SOM neurons across the retinotopic access of the cortex (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D–G).
evidence: This is directly stated based on observations from recordings shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D-G.

claim: The spatial spread of disynaptic inhibition onto PCs exhibits a similar spatial decay as that of excitatory input to SOM neurons.
source: When we examined the spatial spread of disynaptic inhibition onto PCs, inhibition exhibited a similar spatial decay as that of excitatory input to SOM neurons (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by circuit mapping data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B,C.

claim: Long-range coherence involves the summed horizontal dendritic and axonal fields of pyramidal and SOM neurons.
source: These data are consistent with a mechanism for long-range coherence involving the summed horizontal dendritic and axonal fields of pyramidal and SOM neurons.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation based on the spatial mapping data.

claim: The gamma oscillations observed are generated locally by a PING (Pyramidal-Interneuron-Gamma) circuit motif between pyramidal neurons and cortical inhibitory neurons, with SOM neurons playing a critical role.
source: These data support the conclusion that the gamma oscillations we observed here are generated locally by a PING (Pyramidal-Interneuron-Gamma) circuit motif (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Tiesinga and Sejnowski, 2009) between pyramidal neurons and cortical inhibitory neurons, with SOM neurons playing a critical role.
evidence: This is a mechanistic conclusion drawn from the experimental data, referencing established models.

claim: An ING (Interneuron-Gamma) model appears unlikely for the observed oscillations.
source: Because the oscillation is induced by the selective photo-stimulation of excitatory neurons, and since SOM neurons largely lack recurrent synaptic connectivity in L2/3 (Pfeffer et al., 2013), an ING (Interneuron-Gamma) model appears unlikely.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental design and known connectivity patterns, supported by a citation.

claim: Visually induced gamma rhythms in mouse V1 are highly sensitive to SOM neuron suppression.
source: In vivo, visually induced gamma rhythms in mouse V1 are highly sensitive to SOM neuron suppression, whereas PV activity appears to be necessary for circuit stabilization (Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a recent in vivo study, supported by a citation.

claim: PV activity appears to be necessary for circuit stabilization during visually induced gamma rhythms in mouse V1.
source: In vivo, visually induced gamma rhythms in mouse V1 are highly sensitive to SOM neuron suppression, whereas PV activity appears to be necessary for circuit stabilization (Veit et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from a recent in vivo study, supported by a citation.

claim: Gamma rhythms generated locally by a PING network in independent patches of V1 mutually connect to each other via circuits composed of horizontally projecting excitatory axons of L2/3 neurons and SOM neurons.
source: Taken together with previous work showing that L2/3 horizontal axons preferentially recruit SOM neurons (Adesnik et al., 2012), the data presented here support a model for phase-locking spatially separated ensembles across V1. Gamma rhythms, generated locally by a PING network in independent patches of V1, mutually connect to each other via circuits composed of horizontally projecting excitatory axons of L2/3 neurons and SOM neurons, which can extend the range of synchronization through their own horizontal projections.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the current findings and previous work.

claim: SOM neurons can extend the range of synchronization through their own horizontal projections.
source: Gamma rhythms, generated locally by a PING network in independent patches of V1, mutually connect to each other via circuits composed of horizontally projecting excitatory axons of L2/3 neurons and SOM neurons, which can extend the range of synchronization through their own horizontal projections.
evidence: This is part of the proposed mechanistic model based on the findings.

claim: The recruited SOM inhibition synchronizes two ensembles, even over relatively long distances.
source: The recruited SOM inhibition synchronizes the two ensembles, even over relatively long distances.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the long-range coherence experiments.

claim: SOM interneurons are known to be gap junction-coupled.
source: Although it remains to be further explored, since SOM interneurons are known to be gap junction-coupled (Gibson et al., 1999; Hu and Agmon, 2015), electrical connectivity among the SOM population might facilitate or reinforce gamma rhythm generation.
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: Electrical connectivity among the SOM population might facilitate or reinforce gamma rhythm generation.
source: Although it remains to be further explored, since SOM interneurons are known to be gap junction-coupled (Gibson et al., 1999; Hu and Agmon, 2015), electrical connectivity among the SOM population might facilitate or reinforce gamma rhythm generation.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: VIP neurons may influence gamma entrainment by SOM cells, possibly in a state-dependent manner.
source: Additionally, the impact of VIP neurons, which are particularly abundant in L2/3 and project strongly to SOM cells (Pfeffer et al., 2013), may also influence gamma entrainment by SOM cells, possibly in state-dependent manner (Fu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism, supported by citations about VIP-SOM connectivity.

claim: By 450 μm, excitatory input to SOM neurons is 6 ± 2% of its maximum value.
source: When we recorded from SOM cells and mapped their horizontal excitatory input from one side, by 450 μm excitatory input to SOM neurons was 6 ± 2%of its maximum value.
evidence: This is directly stated based on circuit mapping experiments.

claim: Horizontal axons from directly photo-stimulated L2/3 PCs are insufficient to explain long-distance entrainment beyond 450 μm.
source: These measurements probably underestimate the true range of input to SOM neurons due to the sectioning of axons during brain slice preparation, but they do not support the notion that horizontal axons from the directly photo-stimulated L2/3 PCs are sufficient to explain the long-distance entrainment we observe beyond 450 μm.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the circuit mapping data.

claim: SOM cells located between distant ensembles are driven by the sum of input from two sources and synchronize the two ensembles through their own medium range projections.
source: Our results most closely align with the model that SOM cells located between distant ensembles are driven by the sum of the input from the two sources, and synchronize the two ensembles through their own medium range projections.
evidence: This is a mechanistic model proposed based on the circuit mapping data.

claim: This architecture potentially resembles a phase-locked loop control system, with SOM neurons acting as phase comparators.
source: Interestingly, this architecture potentially resembles a phase-locked loop control system, with SOM neurons acting as phase comparators (Ahissar, 1998).
evidence: This is a speculative analogy to engineering control systems, supported by a citation.

claim: For ensembles less than 450 μm apart, horizontal input from each PC ensemble is sufficient to directly drive spiking of SOM cells local to the other ensemble.
source: For more closely spaced ensembles (<450 μm apart), horizontal input from each PC ensemble is sufficient to directly drive spiking of SOM cells local to the other ensemble.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the circuit mapping data showing stronger input at shorter distances.

claim: Synaptic terminal suppression by eNpHR3.0 appears to be effective only early in an action potential train in thalamic axons.
source: Synaptic terminal suppression by eNpHR3.0, though possible here, appears to be effective only early in an action potential train, at least in thalamic axons in which it was tested (Mahn et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study, supported by a citation.

claim: During gamma rhythms, SOM cells fire prolonged spike trains up to 30 Hz.
source: Since, during gamma rhythms, SOM cells fire prolonged spike trains up to 30 Hz, it seems unlikely that the effects we observed would be due to synaptic terminal suppression per se since illuminated axons would be able to maintain transmitter release after the first action potential.
evidence: This is based on the firing rate data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Only a minority of SOM cells in L2/3 of V1 possess long-range horizontal axonal projections.
source: While only a minority of SOM cells in L2/3 of V1 possess long-range horizontal axonal projections (McGarry et al., 2010), as suggested above, these few SOM neurons might be sufficient to help mediate the gamma band coherence.
evidence: This is an anatomical fact from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: A few SOM neurons with long-range horizontal axonal projections might be sufficient to help mediate gamma band coherence.
source: While only a minority of SOM cells in L2/3 of V1 possess long-range horizontal axonal projections (McGarry et al., 2010), as suggested above, these few SOM neurons might be sufficient to help mediate the gamma band coherence.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible mechanism.

claim: In many circuits, both in vivo and in vitro, PV neurons fire and synchronize to gamma rhythms.
source: While our data demonstrate the critical role SOM cells play in horizontally propagating gamma rhythms, in many circuits, both in vivo and in vitro, PV neurons also fire and synchronize to gamma rhythms, and in some cases, are necessary or sufficient to drive gamma rhythmicity (Sohal et al., 2009; Cardin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: In some cases, PV neurons are necessary or sufficient to drive gamma rhythmicity.
source: While our data demonstrate the critical role SOM cells play in horizontally propagating gamma rhythms, in many circuits, both in vivo and in vitro, PV neurons also fire and synchronize to gamma rhythms, and in some cases, are necessary or sufficient to drive gamma rhythmicity (Sohal et al., 2009; Cardin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: The network architecture of L2/3 preferentially recruits SOM cells to fulfill the role of gamma generation.
source: This suggests that while PV neurons or other mechanisms may be sufficient to drive gamma rhythmicity, the network architecture of L2/3 preferentially recruits SOM cells to fulfill this role.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential recruitment of SOM vs PV neurons in the experiments.

claim: Repeating optogenetic experiments with SOM cells can reproduce the same gamma-entraining effects as with PV cells.
source: Moreover, recent results have shown that repeating the exact experiments of these two optogenetic studies with SOM cells could reproduce the same effects, demonstrating that SOM neuron activity is likewise sufficient to entrain gamma on its own (Veit et al., 2017)(Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a finding from recent studies, supported by citations.

claim: SOM neuron activity is sufficient to entrain gamma on its own.
source: Moreover, recent results have shown that repeating the exact experiments of these two optogenetic studies with SOM cells could reproduce the same effects, demonstrating that SOM neuron activity is likewise sufficient to entrain gamma on its own (Veit et al., 2017)(Chen et al., 2017).

claim: Gamma rhythms are phenomenologically diverse, exhibiting a range of peak frequencies, receptive fields, neuron subtype spike-time coupling, and other features.
source: Second, gamma rhythms are phenomenologically diverse, exhibiting a range of peak frequencies, receptive fields, neuron subtype spike-time coupling, and other features (Buzsáki and Wang, 2012; Colgin et al., 2009; Gieselmann and Thiele, 2008; Niell and Stryker, 2010; Ray and Maunsell, 2010; Saleem et al., 2017; Sohal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a known fact from the literature, supported by citations.

claim: The diversity of gamma rhythms strongly suggests diverse underlying mechanisms of oscillation generation and modulation across brain areas and network states.
source: This diversity strongly suggests diverse underlying mechanisms of oscillation generation and modulation across brain areas and network states.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed diversity of gamma rhythms.

claim: PV neuron coupling to gamma rhythms might be a result of gamma entrainment by SOM cells rather than PV neurons generating the gamma rhythm themselves.
source: Third, it is possible that in previous studies that observed tight coupling of PV (or 'fast-spiking' putative PV neurons) to ongoing gamma rhythms, the coupling is actually a result of gamma entrainment by SOM cells (which synapse strongly onto PV neurons) and not due to the PV neurons generating the gamma rhythm themselves.
evidence: This is a speculative reinterpretation of previous findings based on the current results.

claim: In mouse V1, PV neurons strongly couple to visually induced gamma.
source: In mouse V1, PV neurons strongly couple to visually induced gamma, but optogenetically suppressing SOM, but not PV neurons, disrupts gamma rhythms in vivo (Veit et al., 2017), further suggesting this possibility.
evidence: This is a finding from a recent in vivo study, supported by a citation.

claim: Optogenetically suppressing SOM, but not PV neurons, disrupts gamma rhythms in vivo in mouse V1.
source: In mouse V1, PV neurons strongly couple to visually induced gamma, but optogenetically suppressing SOM, but not PV neurons, disrupts gamma rhythms in vivo (Veit et al., 2017), further suggesting this possibility.
evidence: This is a finding from a recent in vivo study, supported by a citation.

claim: During gamma generation, PV neuron spikes are phase-locked to the gamma rhythm.
source: During gamma generation, PV neuron spikes, though sparse, are phase-locked to the gamma rhythm, and as a population may help reinforce the entrainment of local and/or distal excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is based on the phase histogram data shown in Figure 2B and related observations.

claim: PV neurons as a population may help reinforce the entrainment of local and/or distal excitatory neurons during gamma generation.
source: During gamma generation, PV neuron spikes, though sparse, are phase-locked to the gamma rhythm, and as a population may help reinforce the entrainment of local and/or distal excitatory neurons.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about a possible role for PV neurons.

claim: Increasing stimulus sizes trend towards SOM neuron recruitment and away from PV neuron recruitment in vivo.
source: This possibility is balanced with previous data showing that increasing stimulus sizes trend towards SOM neuron recruitment and away from PV neurons recruitment in vivo (Adesnik et al., 2012), which is in agreement with our findings in vitro, and our data showing that inhibition of distal SOM cells essentially abolishes distal entrainment to gamma rhythms.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: Inhibition of distal SOM cells essentially abolishes distal entrainment to gamma rhythms.
source: This possibility is balanced with previous data showing that increasing stimulus sizes trend towards SOM neuron recruitment and away from PV neurons recruitment in vivo (Adesnik et al., 2012), which is in agreement with our findings in vitro, and our data showing that inhibition of distal SOM cells essentially abolishes distal entrainment to gamma rhythms.
evidence: This is based on the optogenetic suppression experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Gamma rhythm generation could involve intracolumnar SOM cells in lower layers.
source: Moreover, although the oscillations we observed were strongly dependent on horizontal connections across L2/3 only (Figure 1G), gamma rhythm generation could involve intracolumnar SOM cells in lower layers as well (Kapfer et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about possible contributions from other layers, supported by a citation.

claim: Horizontal circuits that engage SOM neurons are important for contextual modulation in V1.
source: Horizontal circuits that engage SOM neurons are known to be important for contextual modulation in V1 (Adesnik et al., 2012), and recent data also show them to be critical for size-dependent visually induced gamma rhythms in mouse V1 (Veit et al., 2017), and in the olfactory bulb (Lepousez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from previous studies, supported by citations.

claim: Horizontal circuits that engage SOM neurons are critical for size-dependent visually induced gamma rhythms in mouse V1.
source: Horizontal circuits that engage SOM neurons are known to be important for contextual modulation in V1 (Adesnik et al., 2012), and recent data also show them to be critical for size-dependent visually induced gamma rhythms in mouse V1 (Veit et al., 2017), and in the olfactory bulb (Lepousez et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from a recent study, supported by a citation.

claim: Horizontal circuits that engage SOM neurons are critical for gamma rhythms in the olfactory bulb.

claim: SOM cells target PC dendrites.
source: Moreover, since SOM cells target PC dendrites, their inhibitory action during gamma oscillations could have significant impact on spike timing dependent plasticity in synapses located on distal dendrites.
evidence: This is a known anatomical fact about SOM cell connectivity.

claim: SOM neurons are emerging as critical contributors to both gamma generation and long-range coherence in the cortex.
source: Taken together with our findings that SOM neurons are sufficient for gamma generation within L2/3 and drive gamma-band synchrony in distal neurons, SOM neurons are emerging as critical contributors to both gamma generation and long-range coherence in the cortex.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the current findings and recent literature.

claim: Direct manipulation of SOM neurons or their synaptic partners suggests a new route to probe functional roles of gamma oscillations and gamma-band coherence in visual perception.
source: Moreover, these findings suggest a new route to probe functional roles of gamma oscillations and gamma-band coherence in visual perception: direct manipulation of SOM neurons or their synaptic partners.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about future research directions based on the findings.

claim: In utero electroporation at E15-E16 exclusively labels L2/3 pyramidal cells.
source: Mice were subjected to in utero electroporation at E15-E16 as previously described (Adesnik et al., 2012), which exclusively labels L2/3 pyramidal cells.
evidence: This is a methodological fact supported by a citation and confirmed by histology in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mean peak coherence with 275–400 μm separation is 0.72 ± 0.04.
source: Mean peak coherence with 275–400 μm separation (close): 0.72 ± 0.04, n = 6 pairs; mean peak coherence at 625–850 μm separation (far): 0.44 ± 0.09, n = 7 pairs; mean peak coherence at 275–400 μm with L2/3 cut (cut): 0.11 ± 0.01, n = 11 pairs; p<10−3, Wilcoxon rank sum test between close and cut conditions; p<10−3, Wilcoxon rank sum test between far and cut conditions.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 1J.

claim: Mean firing rate of SOM neurons during photo-induced gamma is 25 ± 5 Hz.
source: Strikingly, targeted loose-patch recordings from SOM and PV neurons in brain slices demonstrated that SOM neurons were reliably driven and tightly correlated with the photo-induced gamma rhythm in L2/3 (Figure 2A–C, n = 10 cells, mean induced rate: 25 ± 5 Hz. Data analyzed from 0 to 1000 ms post-stimulation onset.).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 2.

claim: Mean firing rate of PV neurons during photo-induced gamma is 4 ± 2 Hz.
source: Under the same conditions, the majority of L2/3 PV neurons fired at comparatively low rates or did not fire at all (4 ± 2 Hz, p=0.003, Wilicoxon rank sum test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Suppressing SOM neurons reduces inhibitory gamma power by 74 ± 3.5%.
source: Local suppression of SOM neurons strongly reduced the inhibitory gamma power observed in PCs during photo-induced gamma activity (Figure 3A,B mean power reduction: 74 ± 3.5%, p<10−5, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Suppressing SOM neurons reduces excitatory gamma power by 63 ± 7%.
source: Suppressing SOM cells also desynchronized excitatory synaptic input, demonstrating that their output is critical for pacing the activity of the excitatory network in the gamma band (Figure 3B,C; n = 8 cells, mean power reduction: 63 ± 7%, p=0.004, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 3.

claim: Suppressing PV neurons reduces gamma power by 2.5 ± 6%.
source: In contrast, suppressing PV neurons had no significant effect on gamma power (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–E, n = 9 cells, mean power reduction: 2.5 ± 6%, p=0.25, Wilcoxon signed-rank test), while it did significantly reduce the disynaptic IPSC to a brief pulse of blue light (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F, p=0.016, Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
